news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 7, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology How HPV rewires sugar chemistry in cervical cancer cells by November 6, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 How HPV rewires sugar chemistry in cervical cancer cells Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Cervical cancer remains one of the most common malignancies affecting women worldwide, with an estimated 662,301 new cases and 348,874 deaths recorded globally in 2022 according to GLOBOCAN data. Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus is the principal initiating event in the disease, and sustained expression of the viral E6 and E7 oncoproteins drives malignant transformation and tumor maintenance. Yet viral positivity alone cannot explain why some lesions progress to invasive cancer while others do not, or why established tumors develop resistance to treatment. A new review published in Frontiers in Molecular Biosciences examines whether a chemical modification of proteins, known as O-GlcNAcylation, could connect the metabolic demands imposed by HPV oncogenes to the way cervical cancer cells manage energy production and stress. O-GlcNAcylation is the reversible attachment of a single N-acetylglucosamine sugar to serine or threonine residues on proteins inside the cell. The enzyme O-GlcNAc transferase, or OGT, adds this modification, while O-GlcNAcase, or OGA, removes it. The donor substrate for the reaction, UDP-GlcNAc, is manufactured by the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway from inputs drawn from glucose, glutamine, lipids, and nucleotides. Because the pathway integrates these multiple nutrient streams, O-GlcNAc cycling can report on nutrient availability, biosynthetic demand, and cellular stress without acting as the sole upstream controller of those states. Unlike classical glycosylation in the secretory pathway, this modification occurs on proteins in the nucleus, cytosol, and mitochondrial matrix, and it can respond rapidly to nutrients, oxidative stress, viral infection, and therapeutic pressure. Discover more Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges The review, authored by Yingying Zhang, Yimei Tao, Huirong He, Ping Li, and Minbin Chen, grades the available evidence according to experimental model, temporal context, and causal depth. The authors distinguish between observations made in untreated cervical cancer models, acute responses to treatment, and durable resistance, arguing that these represent distinct biological situations that should not be interpreted interchangeably. Their central conclusion is sobering: cervical cancer studies support links between O-GlcNAcylation and pathways involved in growth and survival, but no mitochondrial O-GlcNAcylation site has been causally validated in HPV-positive cervical cancer. Mechanisms inferred from cardiac, lung, colorectal, and other experimental systems remain hypotheses requiring validation in HPV-positive cervical cancer cells, patient-derived models, and clinical samples. Discover more Engineering job board Research publication platform Scientific instrument sales Laboratory equipment supplier Sustained E6 and E7 expression increases metabolic demand in cervical cancer cells through several established routes. E6 promotes degradation of the p53 tumor suppressor mainly through an E6AP-dependent mechanism, while E7 binds pRB family proteins through its LXCXE motif and releases G1/S checkpoint control. The oncoproteins also engage c-Myc, HIF-1α, PI3K/Akt, PKM2, and E2F-related programs that regulate glycolysis, glutamine utilization, nucleotide synthesis, and adaptation to oxidative stress. Notably, HPV E6 can elevate OGT expression and O-GlcNAcylation, and E6/E7-associated proliferation is accompanied by increased glycolysis and biosynthetic demand. Greater glycolytic activity can alter the availability of hexosamine pathway substrates, but the review stresses that current evidence does not demonstrate that O-GlcNAcylation initiates metabolic reprogramming. The authors position changes in the hexosamine pathway, OGT, and OGA as a potentially responsive and feedback-regulated layer that requires direct flux, substrate, and rescue experiments in HPV-positive models. HPV genotype adds another layer of complexity. HPV16 and HPV18, the predominant oncogenic genotypes in cervical cancer, produce E6 and E7 proteins that differ in sequence, expression control, splice products, and affinity for selected host partners. A common comparison between SiHa cells, which are HPV16-positive squamous carcinoma cells, and HeLa cells, which are HPV18-positive adenocarcinoma cells, confounds viral genotype with histology, integration pattern, viral copy number, and host genomic background. Within the literature surveyed, the authors identified no comparison of matched HPV16 and HPV18 models that quantified hexosamine pathway flux, UDP-GlcNAc abundance, OGT or OGA activity, or site-specific O-GlcNAcylation. An available metabolomic comparison showed features of Warburg metabolism in both cell lines but different nicotinamide and redox profiles: SiHa cells accumulated NAD, NADH, and several glutathione pathway metabolites, whereas HeLa cells showed increased nicotinamide riboside and cysteine. Because the two lines are not isogenic, these differences cannot be assigned to HPV genotype alone. Several cervical cancer findings do reach a higher standard of evidence. Under the review’s classification, two reported relationships meet the Tier 1A criteria, which require a functionally validated O-GlcNAcylation site in a cervical cancer model. Site-directed mutation of NF-κB p65 at Thr322 or Thr352 in HeLa cells reduced CXCR4 expression, and stable OGT depletion reduced lung metastasis in a mouse model. In CaSki cells, which are HPV16-positive, OGT overexpression and depletion, STAT1 knockout, and mutation of Ser727 supported a role for tumor-cell STAT1 O-GlcNAcylation in macrophage polarization and phagocytosis in coculture. However, the study did not examine O-GlcNAcylation within macrophages themselves, and independent replication, in vivo validation, and confirmation in patient-derived samples remain necessary. Other cervical cancer work, including studies linking OGT to E6/E7 promoter activity through host cell factor 1, to epithelial-mesenchymal transition, to PTEN stability through GFPT1, and to cisplatin sensitivity, provides functional evidence without a validated causal modification site and is classified as Tier 1B. The mitochondrial question sits at the heart of the review. Cervical cancer models show variable mitochondrial oxidative activity rather than a consistent reduction in oxidative phosphorylation. In HeLa and SiHa cells and cervical tumor tissues, formation of a mitochondrial complex containing CKS2 and SSBP1 was associated with an OXPHOS-related transcriptional program and chemoradioresistance. Mitochondria therefore remain active contributors to ATP production, ROS signaling, biosynthetic precursor supply, apoptosis control, and stress responses in these tumors. Among all studies included in the review, only one directly manipulated intramitochondrial O-GlcNAcylation: an acute 30-minute intervention in isolated cardiac mitochondria reported changes in Complex I activity, respiratory capacity, and ROS release. Without independent replication or validation in cervical cancer, the authors treat this as preliminary evidence from another model rather than an established mechanism. Candidate mitochondrial substrates identified in other systems illustrate the evidence gap. Drp1, a key mediator of mitochondrial fission, has been shown to be O-GlcNAcylated in non-cervical models, where the modification is associated with mitochondrial recruitment and increased fission, but direct Drp1 O-GlcNAcylation and its functional consequences have not been established in HPV-positive cervical cancer. OPA1, essential for inner-membrane fusion and cristae stability, has been associated with mitochondrial phenotypes involving O-GlcNAcylation in other systems, but current evidence is insufficient to establish it as a direct O-GlcNAcylation substrate. In non-small cell lung cancer, O-GlcNAcylation of HK2 regulated HK2 activity, mitochondrial dynamics, proliferation, and apoptosis, and O-GlcNAcylation of PFK1 altered glucose partitioning with potential effects on antioxidant capacity through the pentose phosphate pathway. These findings identify testable indirect routes by which O-GlcNAcylation could influence mitochondrial redox balance through glucose partitioning without directly modifying mitochondrial proteins, but their relevance to HPV-positive cervical cancer remains untested. Temporal context matters for interpreting treatment-related findings. In HeLa cells, DNA damage acutely recruited OGT to damage sites, and stress-induced increases in O-GlcNAcylation can be transient in other experimental systems. Stable OGT depletion increased cisplatin sensitivity after 24 hours in HeLa cells, and metformin treatment for 24 hours was associated with reduced AMPK O-GlcNAcylation, cell cycle arrest, and apoptosis. Because OGT depletion had been established before cisplatin treatment, the experiment did not test whether cisplatin induced a protective O-GlcNAcylation response. Neither study used a validated resistant model, so the results are described as responses at 24 hours rather than evidence of acquired resistance. The review specifies that acquired resistance in cell models requires repeated drug selection from a sensitive parental line, confirmation that the selected cells are less sensitive than the parental line, and testing of whether resistance persists after drug withdrawal. The authors conclude that current evidence supports individual components of a proposed framework linking E6/E7-associated metabolic demand, hexosamine pathway activity, and substrate-specific O-GlcNAcylation to mitochondrial and immune adaptation, but not the complete causal sequence in HPV-positive cervical cancer. Direct cervical cancer evidence is strongest for selected non-mitochondrial substrates and signaling effects. The principal gap is the absence of site-specific validation of candidate mitochondrial proteins in HPV-positive cervical cancer, together with direct measurements of respiration, ROS, membrane potential, and mitochondrial dynamics. Translational applications, including biomarkers based on O-GlcNAcylation in tissue, blood, cervicovaginal fluid, or extracellular vesicles, and selective combination strategies targeting defined substrates, remain early preclinical or conceptual. Any future intervention must also be evaluated in normal cervical epithelial and immune cells to establish tumor selectivity and exclude impairment of antitumor immunity. O-GlcNAcylation, the review concludes, is best positioned as a context-dependent regulatory layer within a broader network of post-translational modifications rather than as the sole initiator of metabolic reprogramming. The donor substrate for the reaction, UDP-GlcNAc, is manufactured by the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway from inputs drawn from glucose, glutamine, lipids, and nucleotides. analysis.location_and_population: Global, with specific mention of cervical cancer cases and studies involving SiHa and HeLa cells.
analysis.event: A new review published in Frontiers in Molecular Biosciences explores the role of O-GlcNAcylation in cervical cancer cells caused by HPV, focusing on its potential connection to metabolic reprogramming and tumor biology.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The review highlights the metabolic demands of HPV-positive cervical cancer cells, including increased glycolysis and biosynthetic activity, but notes that no mitochondrial O-GlcNAcylation site has been causally validated in these cells. It also emphasizes the need for further studies in patient-derived models and clinical samples.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The review identifies gaps in current evidence and calls for direct flux, substrate, and rescue experiments in HPV-positive models. It also stresses the necessity of independent replication, in vivo validation, and confirmation in patient-derived samples.

analysis.brief_en: A new review published in Frontiers in Molecular Biosciences investigates how human papillomavirus (HPV) influences sugar chemistry in cervical cancer cells through a process called O-GlcNAcylation. The study explores the metabolic demands of HPV-positive cervical cancer cells, noting that while HPV E6 and E7 oncoproteins drive glycolysis and biosynthetic activity, no mitochondrial O-GlcNAcylation site has been causally validated in these cells. The authors emphasize the need for further research, including direct experiments in HPV-positive models and validation in clinical samples. They also highlight the complexity of comparing different HPV genotypes, such as HPV16 and HPV18, due to differences in their biological and genetic characteristics. The review underscores the importance of understanding O-GlcNAcylation's role in cervical cancer progression and treatment resistance, but stresses that current findings remain hypotheses requiring additional validation.

news.content_title: South Africa’s HPV vaccination drive to protect girls from cervical cancer is working
news.content: South Africa introduced a vaccination for human papillomavirus (HPV) in public schools in 2014. The programme offered the vaccination to grade 4 girls aged nine years and older. Uptake was high from the start. About 87% of eligible girls received at least one dose during the first year. By Dorothy Nyemba-Machemedze and Sinead Delany-Moretlwe 2 Nov 2026 0 Human Papillomavirus (HPV) 3D renderings of the human papillomavirus (HPV) capsid (red) against a background image that is an inverted transmission electron micrograph of HPV virus particles harvested and purified from cell culture supernatant. HPV infection can be asymptomatic, cause warts, or disrupt cell growth. 3D rendering by NIH 3D (3d.nih.gov/); micrograph captured at the NIAID Integrated Research Facility (IRF) in Fort Detrick, Maryland. Note: not to scale. Credit: NIAID Almost all cervical cancers are caused by persistent infection with HPV, a very common virus transmitted through sexual contact. Most HPV infections clear naturally, but some high-risk types can persist and can eventually lead to cervical cancer. HPV types 16 and 18 alone are responsible for around 70% of cervical cancer cases worldwide. Cervical cancer is one of the most preventable forms of cancer, yet it remains a major cause of illness and death among women worldwide. Each year, more than 660,000 women are diagnosed globally , and over 90% of new cases and deaths caused by cervical cancer happen in low- and middle-income countries. The challenge is particularly acute in South Africa because HIV increases the risk of HPV infection persisting and progressing to cervical disease. Women living with HIV are much more likely to develop cervical cancer during their lifetime than women without HIV. South Africa had an estimated 7.9 million people living with HIV in mid-2025, accounting for 12.3% of the total population. advertisement Don’t want to see this? Remove ads We are public health researchers dedicated to advancing prevention and treatment of sexually transmitted infections. We evaluated the 2014 vaccination programme’s impact on HPV prevalence among adolescent girls in a setting of high HIV prevalence in South Africa. Our findings were striking. They showed that: infections with HPV types 16 and 18 fell by 83% between pre-vaccine and post-vaccine groups infections with the HPV types responsible for most cervical cancers have fallen by more than 80% among adolescent girls eligible for vaccination, including those living with HIV. This is encouraging news for a country that carries one of the world’s highest burdens of cervical cancer. It also provides important evidence for other African countries with high HIV prevalence that are working towards eliminating cervical cancer as a public health problem. Measuring the impact Because cervical cancer can take decades to develop after HPV infection, it is still too early to measure the programme’s success by looking at cancer rates alone. Instead, our research examined whether vaccine-targeted HPV infections are becoming less common among vaccine-programme eligible generations. A substantial reduction in these infections is a strong early sign that future cervical cancer rates will fall. To assess the programme’s impact, we conducted the HPV One and Two Dose Population Effectiveness (HOPE) study in 2019 and 2023. We compared how common HPV was among adolescent girls aged 17-18 years who were too old to receive the HPV vaccine when the national programme began, with girls of the same age who had been eligible for vaccination through the school-based programme. The study included 2,357 participants recruited from public healthcare facilities across four South African provinces. Importantly, about one-quarter of participants were living with HIV. This allowed us to examine vaccine impact in a population that faces a higher risk of cervical cancer. Our findings Across all participants, infections with HPV types 16 and 18 fell by 83% between pre-vaccine and post-vaccine groups. Before the vaccination programme, about one in five girls carried one of these high-risk HPV types. Among girls eligible for vaccination, that number fell to approximately three in every 100 girls. The programme performed equally well among girls living with HIV. In this group, HPV 16/18 infections fell from 29% to 4%, representing an 82% reduction. We also observed reductions in high-risk HPV types that are genetically related to HPV 16 and 18, a phenomenon known as cross-protection. This increased the overall impact of the vaccination programme. At the same time, other HPV types did not fall. This strengthens confidence that the observed reductions were due to vaccination, not other factors such as changes in sexual behaviour. Another important finding was evidence of indirect protection also known as “herd protection”. Girls in the post-vaccine era who had no documented record of being vaccinated, or did not report having been vaccinated, had much lower rates of HPV 16 and 18 than girls in the pre-vaccine group. This suggests that when most people are vaccinated, the virus spreads much less in the wider community, helping protect unvaccinated individuals. What this means for South Africa and the region The findings provide compelling evidence that South Africa’s HPV vaccination programme is achieving its primary goal: preventing infections that would otherwise place young women at risk of developing cervical cancer later in life. They also demonstrate that the benefits extend to adolescent girls living with HIV, a group that stands to gain substantially from effective cervical cancer prevention. This is especially important for countries in eastern and southern Africa, where both HIV and cervical cancer remain major public health challenges. In 2022, the World Health Organisation recommended a single-dose HPV vaccine for the general population, with the aim of simplifying delivery and increasing global coverage for settings that need it most. Since October 2024, South Africa has adopted a single-dose HPV vaccination approach. Continued monitoring will be important to ensure long-term protection, particularly among people living with HIV. A decade after its introduction, the country’s school-based HPV vaccination programme is delivering measurable population-level benefits and providing a model for other countries seeking to prevent one of the world’s most avoidable cancers. analysis.time: The HPV vaccination programme was introduced in 2014, and the study was conducted in 2019 and 2023. The findings were reported in November 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: South Africa, specifically among adolescent girls aged 17-18 years, with about one-quarter of participants living with HIV.
analysis.event: A school-based HPV vaccination programme was implemented in South Africa in 2014, targeting grade 4 girls aged nine years and older. The programme's impact was evaluated through the HOPE study, showing significant reductions in HPV infections.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: HPV infections with types 16 and 18 fell by 83% among vaccinated and eligible groups. In the HIV-positive group, the reduction was 82%. These findings indicate a substantial impact on reducing the risk of cervical cancer.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The programme's success is being monitored, and continued evaluation is necessary to ensure long-term protection. The study provides evidence of herd protection and cross-protection, but further data is needed to confirm cancer rate reductions.

analysis.brief_en: South Africa’s HPV vaccination programme, introduced in 2014, has shown significant success in reducing infections among adolescent girls. The HOPE study, conducted in 2019 and 2023, found that HPV types 16 and 18 infections fell by 83% in vaccinated groups and 82% in HIV-positive girls. These reductions suggest the programme is effective in preventing cervical cancer, a major public health issue in the country. The study also noted herd protection, where unvaccinated girls had lower infection rates due to widespread vaccination. Despite these positive results, continued monitoring is essential to ensure long-term benefits, especially for those living with HIV. The findings offer a model for other African nations facing similar challenges.

India Proceed with HPV vaccination against cervical cancer only after in-depth study: Jharkhand CM PTI 05 November, 2026 09:45 am IST Follow Us: Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Email Copy Link Stay updated with ThePrint: Preferred Source Google Discover Ranchi, Nov 5 (PTI) Jharkhand Chief Minister Hemant Soren said a comprehensive study was needed before implementing the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination against cervical cancer in the state, while asserting that protecting adolescent girls from the disease was his government’s priority. Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched the National HPV Vaccination Campaign in February, under which 14-year-old girls receive voluntary, free-of-cost, single-dose HPV vaccination with parental consent at government health facilities. Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Mizoram have achieved 100-per cent coverage of their identified target populations under the campaign, while Bihar, Andhra Pradesh and Assam have crossed 90-per cent coverage. Show Full Article In Jharkhand, where the estimated incidence of cervical cancer was 13 cases per 100,000 population, Soren said, “Cervical cancer poses a serious health challenge, and the government will take necessary measures for its prevention and control with the utmost seriousness.” During a meeting with health officials on Wednesday, he said protecting adolescent girls from cervical cancer is a priority for his government, but a decision would be taken only after an in-depth study on HPV vaccination. “Conduct a comprehensive and in-depth study before proceeding with the implementation of HPV vaccination,” the chief minister told the officials and directed them to carry out a state-wide survey. The report prepared after the survey must have detailed data, including the actual number of individuals affected by cervical cancer, their age groups, the various stages of the disease, and the number of active cases, he said. Soren directed health department officials to constitute a committee of experts on the subject, who would hold consultations with directors of reputed medical institutions as well as with cancer specialists and other experts in the relevant field. Emphasising strengthening the regular screening system for timely detection and prevention of cervical cancer, the chief minister said that necessary steps must be taken to improve the availability and accessibility of essential diagnostic facilities at district hospitals and community health centres. news.content_title: Cervical Cancer Prevention Requires More Than HPV Vaccination, Screening Every Two Years Is Essential
news.content: News Issues Wellness Beauty Pharma KOREAN SEARCH Search Health Chosun Cervical Cancer Prevention Requires More Than HPV Vaccination, Screening Every Two Years Is Essential by Jun Jong Bo Updated 2026/11/04 17:25 Photo = Clipart Korea Cancer often develops silently. Although early detection is paramount, treatment is frequently delayed because there are no outward symptoms. The same is true of cervical cancer, a major gynecologic cancer. When persistent high-risk human papillomavirus, HPV, infection causes precancerous lesions, cellular abnormalities can develop, and it may take 15 to 20 years for the disease to progress to cancer. The problem is that symptoms warranting suspicion of cancer rarely appear during this period. This is one of the reasons cervical cancer is often detected late. The best way to detect cervical cancer during the precancer stage is to undergo regular screening. Under the National Cancer Screening Program, cervical cytology tests are provided every two years for women aged 20 and older. While cervical cytology tests examine whether cellular abnormalities are present, HPV DNA tests directly determine whether a person is infected with high-risk HPV that can cause cervical cancer. However, a positive test result does not immediately mean cancer. A secondary screening process is used to identify those who actually belong to the high-risk group among people who test positive, and to determine whether a detailed examination is needed or whether retesting after a certain period is sufficient. Although the importance of screening for early detection continues to grow, the actual screening rate remains low. According to a study by a team led by Professors Kim Jong Yeop and Hong Ji Young of Konyang University, published in the international journal Journal of Gynecologic Oncology in 2024, the rate of regular cervical cancer screening among women in South Korea was only 18.9%. The study followed and analyzed 4663 women for up to 12 years. According to a report by the National Cancer Center, the overall cervical cancer screening rate among women in 2024 was 62%, but the rate among women in their 20s was 40.8%. Delaying screening is not due solely to a lack of interest in the disease. A study analyzing the 2022 Survey on Sexual and Reproductive Health by Life Stage Among Korean Women identified lack of time and the discomfort of gynecologic examinations as major reasons women did not receive gynecologic care. A domestic study published in the Journal of Korean Academy of Nursing also found that women may feel stigma and shame because the virus is transmitted through sexual contact. Experts emphasize that women should undergo regular screening even in the absence of symptoms, since cervical cancer can be detected and managed before it progresses. They explain that it is important not only to check for infection during screening, but also to identify those at high risk of developing a persistent infection and connect them with follow-up care. Professor Lee Jae Kwan of the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology at Korea University Guro Hospital said, “Cervical cancer is preventable, but vaccination alone is not enough. The success of prevention depends on regular screening and early detection, follow-up evaluation, and continued treatment.” This article has been translated AI. by Jun Jong Bo View All Articles Copyright © Health Chosun. news.content_title: Karonga Expands Cervical Cancer Prevention With HPV Vaccination
news.content: Vaccination in Progress. Picture by Naomi Tadala Magawa. Mana KARONGA, Malawi — Efforts to reduce cervical cancer deaths in Karonga District have gained momentum with the introduction of human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination alongside existing screening services, writes Naomi Tadala Magawa, MANA. The initiative, implemented by Belgian fifth-year medical student Anais Hublet in collaboration with Lusubilo Community Care and the Karonga Diocese, aims to prevent HPV infections and promote early detection of cervical cancer. Hublet said the introduction of vaccination marked an important step in strengthening the programme, which initially focused on screening women. The initiative targets two areas: vaccinating 9-year-old girls against HPV to reduce their risk of developing cervical cancer later in life, and screening women to support early detection and treatment. “The major purpose is to decrease the number of women dying from cervical cancer. We are approaching prevention in two ways which are vaccination which gives young girls a very low chance of developing the cancer later in life and screening, which helps detect the disease early,” she said. Hublet said the screening programme had recorded an increase in participation, from 92 women in its first year, three years ago, to 800 last year. She said the long-term goal was to make the programme operate throughout the year, even in her absence, as locally trained nurses had the skills to continue providing the services. “We are hoping that it would go on the whole year, even if I am not here, because the nurses are from Malawi and the materials are from Malawi, so it can work without me,” she said. A nurse-midwife at Karonga District Hospital, Shida Gomeka, said HPV vaccination was important in preventing infections associated with most cervical cancer cases. “The HPV vaccine will help a lot because it reduces the number of women who can have HPV on their cervix,” she said. Gomeka said screening was also essential because HPV infections often develop without noticeable symptoms, making it difficult for women to know their status without testing. She said screening helps health workers identify women who test negative for HPV, those who test positive and those who may already show signs of cervical cancer, enabling them to receive appropriate care. Gomeka urged men to support prevention efforts by encouraging their wives, mothers, sisters and children to access screening and vaccination services. She said preventing cervical cancer should be a shared responsibility involving both men and women

news.content_original: Vaccination in Progress. Picture by Naomi Tadala Magawa. Mana KARONGA, Malawi — Efforts to reduce cervical cancer deaths in Karonga District have gained momentum with the introduction of human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination alongside existing screening services, writes Naomi Tadala Magawa, MANA. The initiative, implemented by Belgian fifth-year medical student Anais Hublet in collaboration with Lusubilo Community Care and the Karonga Diocese, aims to prevent HPV infections and promote early detection of cervical cancer. Hublet said the introduction of vaccination marked an important step in strengthening the programme, which initially focused on screening women. The initiative targets two areas: vaccinating 9-year-old girls against HPV to reduce their risk of developing cervical cancer later in life, and screening women to support early detection and treatment. “The major purpose is to decrease the number of women dying from cervical cancer. We are approaching prevention in two ways which are vaccination which gives young girls a very low chance of developing the cancer later in life and screening, which helps detect the disease early,” she said. Hublet said the screening programme had recorded an increase in participation, from 92 women in its first year, three years ago, to 800 last year. She said the long-term goal was to make the programme operate throughout the year, even in her absence, as locally trained nurses had the skills to continue providing the services. “We are hoping that it would go on the whole year, even if I am not here, because the nurses are from Malawi and the materials are from Malawi, so it can work without me,” she said. A nurse-midwife at Karonga District Hospital, Shida Gomeka, said HPV vaccination was important in preventing infections associated with most cervical cancer cases. “The HPV vaccine will help a lot because it reduces the number of women who can have HPV on their cervix,” she said. Gomeka said screening was also essential because HPV infections often develop without noticeable symptoms, making it difficult for women to know their status without testing. She said screening helps health workers identify women who test negative for HPV, those who test positive and those who may already show signs of cervical cancer, enabling them to receive appropriate care. Gomeka urged men to support prevention efforts by encouraging their wives, mothers, sisters and children to access screening and vaccination services. She said preventing cervical cancer should be a shared responsibility involving both men and women

If you have a patient with recurrent or recalcitrant verruca vulgaris, you may have heard of using the HPV vaccine as treatment. There is biologic rationale for this approach; however, there is an important caveat: The HPV types that cause verruca vulgaris are different than the ones targeted by the 9-valent vaccine. Despite this mismatch, observational studies and case studies have suggested that the HPV vaccine may provide cross-protective immunity, which may potentially help clear or prevent cutaneous warts. Article Key Points Verruca vulgaris HPV types ≠ 9-valent vaccine types. Cross-protective immunity may help clear/prevent cutaneous warts. Evidence = observational studies + small trials; no FDA approval. Continue HPV vaccination for approved indications only. Larger RCTs needed before standard-of-care use for warts. Dive Deeper What mechanisms explain HPV vaccine cross-protection for cutaneous warts? Which wart subtypes respond best to HPV vaccination? How effective is HPV vaccine vs standard wart therapies? See clinical implications for practiceSummarize this article in patient-friendly language However, this is not an FDA-approved treatment, and the evidence largely consists of observational studies and small trials. SUGGESTED FOR YOU For primary care, continue to recommend the HPV vaccine for its approved indications. However, we do need larger, randomized controlled trials before considering it standard of care for verruca vulgaris. Dive Deeper See clinical implications for practice Summarize this article in patient-friendly language Commonly Asked by HCPs Q: What are the approved indications, safety considerations, and age-based recommendations for HPV vaccination? A: HPV vaccines are recommended according to age, prior vaccination status, and routine preventive guidelines, with the main goal of preventing HPV-related disease rather than treating existing warts. Safety is generally well established for approved use, but clinicians should distinguish preventive vaccination from off-label wart treatment because evidence for the latter remains limited. Read full answer Q: What is the evidence for cross-protective immunity from HPV vaccines against skin warts? A: The biologic rationale is that some HPV vaccine responses may generate partial cross-reactive immunity, but the vaccine targets oncogenic and mucosal HPV types rather than the cutaneous types that commonly cause verruca vulgaris. Available data are mostly case reports, small studies, and observational series, so efficacy remains uncertain and not yet guideline-endorsed for wart treatment. Read full answer Q: How are recurrent or recalcitrant verruca vulgaris managed in primary care? A: Primary care management of recurrent warts usually starts with confirming the diagnosis, using standard wart therapies, and setting expectations about slow response and recurrence. Common approaches include topical keratolytics, cryotherapy, and watchful waiting in selected cases, with escalation based on lesion burden, location, persistence, and patient preference. Read full answer Q: When should clinicians consider HPV vaccination for cutaneous wart prevention or recurrence? A: HPV vaccination is routinely recommended for its approved preventive indications, but its use for cutaneous wart prevention or treatment remains off-label and investigational. Research interest centers on whether vaccine-induced cross-reactive immunity might help reduce wart burden, yet current evidence is not strong enough to make it standard therapy for verruca vulgaris. Read full answer Q: Which patients with difficult-to-treat warts warrant dermatology referral or immunodeficiency evaluation? A: Patients with extensive, painful, treatment-resistant, or atypical warts may need dermatology referral to confirm diagnosis and consider additional therapies. Recurrent or severe warts can also prompt consideration of underlying immune dysfunction, especially when lesions are numerous, widespread, or accompanied by other recurrent infections. If you have a patient with recurrent or recalcitrant verruca vulgaris, you may have heard of using the HPV vaccine as treatment. There is biologic rationale for this approach; however, there is an important caveat: The HPV types that cause verruca vulgaris are different than the ones targeted by the 9-valent vaccine. Despite this mismatch, observational studies and case studies have suggested that the HPV vaccine may provide cross-protective immunity, which may potentially help clear or prevent cutaneous warts. Article Key Points Verruca vulgaris HPV types ≠ 9-valent vaccine types. Cross-protective immunity may help clear/prevent cutaneous warts. Evidence = observational studies + small trials; no FDA approval. Continue HPV vaccination for approved indications only. Larger RCTs needed before standard-of-care use for warts. Dive Deeper What mechanisms explain HPV vaccine cross-protection for cutaneous warts? Which wart subtypes respond best to HPV vaccination? How effective is HPV vaccine vs standard wart therapies? See clinical implications for practiceSummarize this article in patient-friendly language However, this is not an FDA-approved treatment, and the evidence largely consists of observational studies and small trials. SUGGESTED FOR YOU For primary care, continue to recommend the HPV vaccine for its approved indications. However, we do need larger, randomized controlled trials before considering it standard of care for verruca vulgaris. Dive Deeper See clinical implications for practice Summarize this article in patient-friendly language Commonly Asked by HCPs Q: What are the approved indications, safety considerations, and age-based recommendations for HPV vaccination? A: HPV vaccines are recommended according to age, prior vaccination status, and routine preventive guidelines, with the main goal of preventing HPV-related disease rather than treating existing warts. Safety is generally well established for approved use, but clinicians should distinguish preventive vaccination from off-label wart treatment because evidence for the latter remains limited. Read full answer Q: What is the evidence for cross-protective immunity from HPV vaccines against skin warts? A: The biologic rationale is that some HPV vaccine responses may generate partial cross-reactive immunity, but the vaccine targets oncogenic and mucosal HPV types rather than the cutaneous types that commonly cause verruca vulgaris. Available data are mostly case reports, small studies, and observational series, so efficacy remains uncertain and not yet guideline-endorsed for wart treatment. Read full answer Q: How are recurrent or recalcitrant verruca vulgaris managed in primary care? A: Primary care management of recurrent warts usually starts with confirming the diagnosis, using standard wart therapies, and setting expectations about slow response and recurrence. Common approaches include topical keratolytics, cryotherapy, and watchful waiting in selected cases, with escalation based on lesion burden, location, persistence, and patient preference. Read full answer Q: When should clinicians consider HPV vaccination for cutaneous wart prevention or recurrence? A: HPV vaccination is routinely recommended for its approved preventive indications, but its use for cutaneous wart prevention or treatment remains off-label and investigational. Research interest centers on whether vaccine-induced cross-reactive immunity might help reduce wart burden, yet current evidence is not strong enough to make it standard therapy for verruca vulgaris. Read full answer Q: Which patients with difficult-to-treat warts warrant dermatology referral or immunodeficiency evaluation? A: Patients with extensive, painful, treatment-resistant, or atypical warts may need dermatology referral to confirm diagnosis and consider additional therapies. Recurrent or severe warts can also prompt consideration of underlying immune dysfunction, especially when lesions are numerous, widespread, or accompanied by other recurrent infections. A new review published in Virology Journal examines how the bacterial communities inhabiting the female reproductive tract may tip the balance between viral clearance and cancer development, focusing on the immunoregulatory role of these microbes during HPV-associated cervical carcinogenesis and the oncogenic effects of microbial dysbiosis. The review, authored by Dongfang Fu, Tengge Yu and Yinghong Zheng, argues that the vaginal microbiota is not a passive bystander in HPV infection. According to the authors, the presence and abundance of certain bacterial species may confer protective effects against HPV infection and facilitate viral clearance, thereby reducing the risk of precancerous lesions in the cervix, vagina and vulva. Conversely, other bacterial taxa may contribute to the promotion of pathological conditions, creating a microbial environment that favours viral persistence and lesion progression. This dual role places the microbiome at the centre of one of the most important unresolved questions in HPV biology: why some infections resolve spontaneously while others progress toward malignancy. The authors note that genetic and environmental factors underlying these differential outcomes remain an active area of investigation, with the microbiome emerging as a critical element that may modulate this balance by either promoting or inhibiting viral infection. Discover more See an OB-GYN Find Cancer Care cancer Cancer Elucidating the composition of the vaginal microbiota and its dysbiotic alterations in relation to HPV infection and persistence may therefore enhance the predictive accuracy regarding infection outcomes. The precise identification of bacterial components associated with HPV-induced pathology also holds potential clinical relevance and may inform alternative therapeutic strategies. Technological capability underpins this growing field. The authors highlight that current advancements enable rapid, high-throughput analysis of the vaginal microbiome, which can be applied in longitudinal studies to delineate the roles of specific bacterial species in the initiation, prevention, progression or regression of HPV-related cervical, vaginal and vulvar lesions. As a review, the article synthesises existing research progress rather than presenting new experimental data, and its conclusions describe associations and hypotheses that require testing in longitudinal and interventional studies. The authors position the microbiome as a critical element that may modulate the balance between viral clearance and cancer development, a balance whose genetic and environmental determinants are still being mapped. Discover more cancers Track Fertility Study Anatomy Check Symptoms Book a Checkup The composition of the vaginal microbiota, its dysbiotic shifts and the specific bacterial species involved may all influence whether high-risk HPV infection ends in clearance, persists silently or advances along the pathway toward cervical, vaginal or vulvar cancer, making microbiome characterisation an increasingly relevant tool in understanding and potentially predicting the course of HPV-associated disease. Subject of Research: The immunoregulatory role of the female reproductive tract microbiota in HPV-associated cervical carcinogenesis and the oncogenic effects of microbial dysbiosis. analysis.brief_en: A review published in Virology Journal on November 4, 2026, explores how the vaginal microbiota may influence the outcomes of human papillomavirus (HPV) infections. The study, authored by Dongfang Fu, Tengge Yu, and Yinghong Zheng, argues that the presence and abundance of certain bacterial species can confer protective effects against HPV, promoting viral clearance and reducing the risk of precancerous lesions in the cervix, vagina, and vulva. Conversely, other bacterial taxa may contribute to viral persistence and lesion progression. The review notes that the microbiome plays a critical role in modulating the balance between viral clearance and cancer development, though the exact mechanisms remain under investigation. It does not present new experimental data but synthesises existing research, highlighting the need for further studies to validate these associations. The findings suggest that understanding the vaginal microbiota could enhance the prediction of HPV infection outcomes and inform potential therapeutic strategies.

news.content_zh: 2026 年 11 月 4 日在《病毒学杂志》上发表的一篇评论探讨了阴道微生物群如何影响 人乳头瘤病毒 (HPV) 感染的结果。这项由 Dongfang Fu、Tengge Yu 和 Yinghong Cheng 撰写的研究认为,某些细菌种类的存在和丰富可以对 HPV 产生保护作用,促进病毒清除并降低子宫颈、阴道和外阴癌前病变的风险。相反,其他细菌类群可能有助于病毒持续存在和病变进展。该评论指出,微生物组在调节病毒清除和癌症发展之间的平衡方面发挥着关键作用,尽管确切的机制仍在研究中。它没有提供新的实验数据,而是综合了现有的研究,强调需要进一步研究来验证这些关联。研究结果表明,了解阴道微生物群可以增强 HPV 感染结果的预测并为潜在的治疗策略提供信息。

news.content_title: Translational Data from Anal Cancer Patients Show Pelareorep Drives HPV-Specific Immune Responses, Supporting its Potential Across HPV-Driven Cancers
news.content: Pelareorep-driven changes in the tumor microenvironment are associated with tumor responses and shrinkage Immune activation levels more than doubled in nearly all patients after one cycle of treatment Substantial increases in HPV-16-specific T cells and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes observed when pelareorep is combined with a checkpoint inhibitor SAN DIEGO, Nov. 04, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Oncolytics Biotech® Inc. (Nasdaq: ONCY) ("Oncolytics” or the "Company”), a clinical-stage immunotherapy company developing pelareorep, today announced new translational data from an ongoing study showing pelareorep’s ability to increase human papillomavirus ("HPV”)-16-specific T cell clones and tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte ("TIL”) clones in second-line or later squamous cell anal cancer ("SCAC”) patients at the Society for Immunotherapy of Cancer ("SITC”) 2026 Annual Meeting. Pelareorep combined with a checkpoint inhibitor generated promising efficacy signals in second-line or later SCAC, including more than doubling the objective response rate and increasing median duration of response by 50% compared to the current approved therapy in that patient population. Multiple analyses help explain how pelareorep generates innate and adaptive immune responses and synergizes with other therapies. Highlights from the SITC abstract include: - In seven of eight evaluable patients, greater than two-fold increases in levels of the immune-activation biomarkers CXCL10, IFN-γ, and soluble PD-L1 were observed after one cycle of therapy. - After three cycles of treatment, all four evaluable patients saw expansion of TIL clones in peripheral blood, which was associated with reductions in tumor size, including two complete responses and two partial responses. - The four responding patients with TIL expansion also demonstrated significant expansion of at least one HPV-16-specific T cell clone. - Among 14 patients evaluated for HPV-16-specific immune responses, six showed HPV-16 clonal expansion, and four of those patients experienced tumor shrinkage. - The Phase 1/2, Simon 2-stage study is assessing the safety and efficacy of pelareorep in combination with a checkpoint inhibitor in second-line or later unresectable SCAC patients. "These data reinforce pelareorep’s potential in multiple HPV-driven cancers as those tumor types generally exhibit low response rates to checkpoint inhibitors,” said Thomas Heineman, MD, PhD, Chief Medical Officer of Oncolytics. "Pelareorep’s ability to increase tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte populations and expand HPV-specific T cells form the basis for its synergy with checkpoint inhibitors and reinforces the potential of this combination to combat tumor growth in HPV-associated cancers. More broadly, these data support our belief in pelareorep as a backbone immunotherapy capable of activating anti-tumor immunity and improving responses to multiple therapies across a wide range of tumor types.” "We see HPV-associated cancers as a compelling business development opportunity for pelareorep, spanning anal, HPV-positive oropharyngeal, cervical, and other malignancies and representing a potential $3 to 5 billion market based on our internal estimates,” said Jared Kelly, Chief Executive Officer of Oncolytics. "The combination of HPV-specific T cell expansion in our anal cancer study and prior clinical efficacy signals in head and neck cancer gives prospective partners a differentiated scientific and clinical rationale to explore pelareorep alongside checkpoint inhibitors. With systemic delivery, substantial clinical experience, and the potential to pursue multiple indications, we believe pelareorep offers a scalable opportunity to extend immunotherapy franchises into underserved patient populations. Our priority is to translate this evidence into strategic collaborations that can accelerate development and realize the broader commercial opportunity.” About Pelareorep Pelareorep is an intravenously delivered, systemically active, investigational immunotherapy with a dual mechanism of action that selectively replicates in tumor cells while activating both innate and adaptive anti-tumor immune responses, including the upregulation of key inflammatory cytokines resulting in the formation of tertiary lymphoid structures and the expansion of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. It has been administered to over 1,200 patients, and clinical studies have demonstrated pelareorep’s potential to enhance the activity of checkpoint inhibitors and other anti-cancer therapies across multiple solid tumor types. About Oncolytics Biotech Inc. Oncolytics is a clinical-stage biotechnology company developing pelareorep, an investigational intravenously delivered double-stranded RNA immunotherapeutic agent. Pelareorep has demonstrated encouraging results in multiple first-line pancreatic cancer studies, two randomized Phase 2 studies in metastatic breast cancer, and early-phase studies in anal and colorectal cancer. It is designed to induce anti-cancer immune responses by converting immunologically inactive tumors to active through the activation of innate and adaptive immune responses. news.content_original: Pelareorep-driven changes in the tumor microenvironment are associated with tumor responses and shrinkage Immune activation levels more than doubled in nearly all patients after one cycle of treatment Substantial increases in HPV-16-specific T cells and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes observed when pelareorep is combined with a checkpoint inhibitor SAN DIEGO, Nov. 04, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Oncolytics Biotech® Inc. (Nasdaq: ONCY) ("Oncolytics” or the "Company”), a clinical-stage immunotherapy company developing pelareorep, today announced new translational data from an ongoing study showing pelareorep’s ability to increase human papillomavirus ("HPV”)-16-specific T cell clones and tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte ("TIL”) clones in second-line or later squamous cell anal cancer ("SCAC”) patients at the Society for Immunotherapy of Cancer ("SITC”) 2026 Annual Meeting. Pelareorep combined with a checkpoint inhibitor generated promising efficacy signals in second-line or later SCAC, including more than doubling the objective response rate and increasing median duration of response by 50% compared to the current approved therapy in that patient population. Multiple analyses help explain how pelareorep generates innate and adaptive immune responses and synergizes with other therapies. Highlights from the SITC abstract include: - In seven of eight evaluable patients, greater than two-fold increases in levels of the immune-activation biomarkers CXCL10, IFN-γ, and soluble PD-L1 were observed after one cycle of therapy. - After three cycles of treatment, all four evaluable patients saw expansion of TIL clones in peripheral blood, which was associated with reductions in tumor size, including two complete responses and two partial responses. - The four responding patients with TIL expansion also demonstrated significant expansion of at least one HPV-16-specific T cell clone. - Among 14 patients evaluated for HPV-16-specific immune responses, six showed HPV-16 clonal expansion, and four of those patients experienced tumor shrinkage. - The Phase 1/2, Simon 2-stage study is assessing the safety and efficacy of pelareorep in combination with a checkpoint inhibitor in second-line or later unresectable SCAC patients. "These data reinforce pelareorep’s potential in multiple HPV-driven cancers as those tumor types generally exhibit low response rates to checkpoint inhibitors,” said Thomas Heineman, MD, PhD, Chief Medical Officer of Oncolytics. "Pelareorep’s ability to increase tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte populations and expand HPV-specific T cells form the basis for its synergy with checkpoint inhibitors and reinforces the potential of this combination to combat tumor growth in HPV-associated cancers. More broadly, these data support our belief in pelareorep as a backbone immunotherapy capable of activating anti-tumor immunity and improving responses to multiple therapies across a wide range of tumor types.” "We see HPV-associated cancers as a compelling business development opportunity for pelareorep, spanning anal, HPV-positive oropharyngeal, cervical, and other malignancies and representing a potential $3 to 5 billion market based on our internal estimates,” said Jared Kelly, Chief Executive Officer of Oncolytics. "The combination of HPV-specific T cell expansion in our anal cancer study and prior clinical efficacy signals in head and neck cancer gives prospective partners a differentiated scientific and clinical rationale to explore pelareorep alongside checkpoint inhibitors. With systemic delivery, substantial clinical experience, and the potential to pursue multiple indications, we believe pelareorep offers a scalable opportunity to extend immunotherapy franchises into underserved patient populations. Our priority is to translate this evidence into strategic collaborations that can accelerate development and realize the broader commercial opportunity.” About Pelareorep Pelareorep is an intravenously delivered, systemically active, investigational immunotherapy with a dual mechanism of action that selectively replicates in tumor cells while activating both innate and adaptive anti-tumor immune responses, including the upregulation of key inflammatory cytokines resulting in the formation of tertiary lymphoid structures and the expansion of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. It has been administered to over 1,200 patients, and clinical studies have demonstrated pelareorep’s potential to enhance the activity of checkpoint inhibitors and other anti-cancer therapies across multiple solid tumor types. elements_zh.location_and_population: 该研究是在二线或晚期鳞状细胞肛门癌(SCAC)患者的背景下进行的。该分析的重点是 pelareorep 在 HPV 相关癌症中的潜力,包括肛门癌、口咽癌、宫颈癌和其他恶性肿瘤。该研究是 1/2 期 Simon 2 阶段试验的一部分,该试验评估 pelareorep 与检查点抑制剂联合治疗二线或后期不可切除 SCAC 患者的安全性和有效性。
elements_zh.event: 一项正在进行的研究的新转化数据表明,pelareorep 可增加二线或晚期鳞状细胞肛门癌 (SCAC) 患者的 HPV-16 特异性 T 细胞克隆和肿瘤浸润淋巴细胞 (TIL) 克隆。这些数据已在癌症免疫治疗协会 (SITC) 2026 年年会上公布。该研究还表明,pelareorep 与检查点抑制剂联合产生了有希望的疗效信号,与该患者群体中目前批准的疗法相比,客观缓解率增加了一倍以上,中位缓解持续时间延长了 50%。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 在 14 名接受 HPV-16 特异性 免疫应答 评估的患者中,6 名患者出现 HPV-16 克隆扩增,其中 4 名患者出现肿瘤缩小。在 8 名可评估患者中,有 7 名患者在一个治疗周期后观察到免疫激活生物标志物 CXCL10、IFN-γ 和可溶性 PD-L1 水平增加了两倍以上。经过三个周期的 治疗 治疗后,所有四名可评估患者均观察到外周血中 TIL 克隆的扩增,这与肿瘤大小的减小相关,包括两个完全缓解和两个部分缓解。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 该研究正在进行中,是 1/2 期西蒙 2 阶段试验的一部分。该公司正在推进 pelareorep 与化疗和/或检查点抑制剂联合治疗转移性胃肠道癌症,该药物已获得美国食品和药物管理局针对结直肠癌、肛门癌和胰腺癌的快速通道指定。该公司正在积极寻求战略合作伙伴关系,以加速发展并最大限度地提高商业影响。

analysis_zh.time: Pelarorep 驱动的肿瘤微环境变化与肿瘤反应和缩小有关。在 治疗 一个周期后,几乎所有患者的免疫激活水平都增加了一倍以上。当 pelareorep 与检查点抑制剂联合使用时,观察到 HPV-16 特异性 T 细胞和肿瘤浸润淋巴细胞大幅增加。2026 年 04 月(环球通讯社)——Oncolytics Biotech® Inc.
analysis_zh.location_and_population: 该研究是在二线或晚期鳞状细胞肛门癌(SCAC)患者的背景下进行的。该分析的重点是 pelareorep 在 HPV 相关癌症中的潜力,包括肛门癌、口咽癌、宫颈癌和其他恶性肿瘤。该研究是 1/2 期 Simon 2 阶段试验的一部分,该试验评估 pelareorep 与检查点抑制剂联合治疗二线或后期不可切除 SCAC 患者的安全性和有效性。
analysis_zh.event: 一项正在进行的研究的新转化数据表明,pelareorep 可增加二线或晚期鳞状细胞肛门癌 (SCAC) 患者的 HPV-16 特异性 T 细胞克隆和肿瘤浸润淋巴细胞 (TIL) 克隆。这些数据已在癌症免疫治疗协会 (SITC) 2026 年年会上公布。该研究还表明,pelareorep 与检查点抑制剂联合产生了有希望的疗效信号,与该患者群体中目前批准的疗法相比,客观缓解率增加了一倍以上,中位缓解持续时间延长了 50%。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 在 14 名接受 HPV-16 特异性 免疫应答 评估的患者中,6 名患者出现 HPV-16 克隆扩增,其中 4 名患者出现肿瘤缩小。在 8 名可评估患者中,有 7 名患者在一个治疗周期后观察到免疫激活生物标志物 CXCL10、IFN-γ 和可溶性 PD-L1 水平增加了两倍以上。经过三个周期的 治疗 治疗后,所有四名可评估患者均观察到外周血中 TIL 克隆的扩增,这与肿瘤大小的减小相关,包括两个完全缓解和两个部分缓解。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 该研究正在进行中,是 1/2 期西蒙 2 阶段试验的一部分。该公司正在推进 pelareorep 与化疗和/或检查点抑制剂联合治疗转移性胃肠道癌症,该药物已获得美国食品和药物管理局针对结直肠癌、肛门癌和胰腺癌的快速通道指定。该公司正在积极寻求战略合作伙伴关系,以加速发展并最大限度地提高商业影响。

Oncology/Hematology > Other Cancers De-Escalated Treatment for HPV-Related Throat Cancer Gets Long-Term Supporting Data — More than 90% of patients alive without evidence of disease at 5 years by Charles Bankhead, Senior Editor, MedPage Today November 3, 2026 • 4 min read Add MedPage Today on Google MedpageToday Key Takeaways De-escalated treatment for HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer achieved durable cancer control in over 90% of patients. Treatment reduced elective nodal radiation to 30 Gy and omitted low-risk nodal regions without failures. The results add to existing evidence supporting de-escalation for HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer but this particular regimen still requires confirmation in a multicenter phase III trial. Reduced-intensity treatment for human papillomavirus (HPV)-positive oropharyngeal cancer (OPC) led to durable cancer control in more than 90% of patients, long-term follow-up from a prospective study showed. After a median follow-up of 5 years, 94% of patients had no evidence of disease and 90.6% were alive at last follow-up after de-escalated elective nodal irradiation (ENI) during definitive concurrent chemoradiation (CRT). Five-year locoregional control, distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS), and overall survival (OS) exceeded 90%. All but one patient with locoregional failure had recurrences in areas with known residual macroscopic disease. No treatment failures occurred in nodal basins that were omitted from treatment. De-escalation came in the form of 30-Gy ENI instead of the usual 50-60 Gy dose and omission of low-risk nodal basins, reported Nancy Y. Lee, MD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City, and colleagues in JAMA Oncologyopens in a new tab or window. "These outcomes were attained across the spectrum of T- and N-stage groups and smoking histories among patients predominantly treated with concurrent platinum-based chemoradiosensitization," the authors noted. "The systematic omission of uninvolved nodal levels IB/V did not result in failures in those areas and provides a simple class solution to reducing irradiated volume and toxic effects. The 30-Gy ENI dose remains the lowest among published approaches, is tailored to HPV-associated disease, and results in the lowest reported gastrostomy tube insertion rate." "Although low-dose ENI without concurrent chemotherapy has been investigated, recent phase III randomized trials have demonstrated the superiority of concurrent platinum-based chemotherapy for achieving cure in HPV-associated OPC, underscoring the importance of de-escalating ENI within an optimally curative paradigm for HPV-associated OPC," they wrote. The study showed that focusing on radiation dose is not the only strategy to de-escalate treatment for HPV-associated OPC, said David Sher, MD, of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, who was not involved in the study. "While we often focus on the total dose delivered to visible cancer, in actuality, ENI is responsible for a substantial amount of normal tissue irradiation and dose to critical normal structures, such as the salivary glands and swallowing structures," Sher, an expert for the American Society for Radiation Oncology, told MedPage Today. "There has been a progressive recognition that ENI dose can be a significant contributor to quality-of-life outcomes, and there are several studies, both prospective and retrospective, that have shown that the standard dose of 50 Gy can be substantially lowered." "Although we do not have quality-of-life data from this study, prior reports were also very favorable." Providing additional context for the study results, Sher noted that all patients underwent PET-CT imaging and the vast majority had MRI as well. Such advanced imaging may play a key role in identifying smaller lymph nodes that might harbor cancer and require higher radiation doses. Additionally, all the patients received cisplatin-containing chemotherapy, and HPV-associated OPC is cisplatin sensitive. Also, the authors did not report how many "equivocal" lymph nodes were treated with a higher radiation dose. Results of the current study add to those of a previous phase III trial that used a slightly higher nodal irradiation dose, he added. "All of this work strongly suggests we are delivering ENI doses that are far too high, and we need to be more aggressive in reducing the acute and long-term side-effect burden of our treatments while preserving oncologic efficacy," said Sher. "For such a result to become a true standard of care, though, we do need a phase III randomized study to confirm non-inferiority in a multi-institutional setting, and hopefully such a trial can be available soon to patients and our community." Lee and colleagues previously reportedopens in a new tab or window 2-year outcomes with the de-escalation strategy, showing good locoregional control and survival with "excellent" quality of life. The current report aimed to establish the durability of the strategy, as assessed after a median follow-up of 5 years. The analysis involved 276 patients treated with intensity-modulated radiotherapy (n=256) or intensity-modulated proton therapy (n=20). Treated nodal and subclinical regions received 30 Gy in 15 fractions and a sequential boost of 40 Gy in 20 fractions. The 5-year results showed that 260 patients had no evidence of disease at 5 years and 250 were alive at last follow-up. Five-year outcomes were: Locoregional control: 97.0% OS: 90.8% Progression-free survival: 85.9% DMFS: 91.2% A single elective nodal failure occurred 6 months after concurrent CRT in a contralateral indeterminate lymph node present at baseline and treated with 30 Gy, the authors reported. The last regional failure occurred 18 months post-treatment. Distant-only recurrences occurred in 23 patients. At last follow-up, 12 of the patients remained alive with no evidence of disease, and one remained alive with disease. Please enable JavaScript to view the comments powered by Disqus. Providing additional context for the study results, Sher noted that all patients underwent PET-CT imaging and the vast majority had MRI as well. Such advanced imaging may play a key role in identifying smaller lymph nodes that might harbor cancer and require higher radiation doses. Additionally, all the patients received cisplatin-containing chemotherapy, and HPV-associated OPC is cisplatin sensitive. Also, the authors did not report how many "equivocal" lymph nodes were treated with a higher radiation dose. Results of the current study add to those of a previous phase III trial that used a slightly higher nodal irradiation dose, he added. "All of this work strongly suggests we are delivering ENI doses that are far too high, and we need to be more aggressive in reducing the acute and long-term side-effect burden of our treatments while preserving oncologic efficacy," said Sher. "For such a result to become a true standard of care, though, we do need a phase III randomized study to confirm non-inferiority in a multi-institutional setting, and hopefully such a trial can be available soon to patients and our community." Lee and colleagues previously reportedopens in a new tab or window 2-year outcomes with the de-escalation strategy, showing good locoregional control and survival with "excellent" quality of life. The current report aimed to establish the durability of the strategy, as assessed after a median follow-up of 5 years. The analysis involved 276 patients treated with intensity-modulated radiotherapy (n=256) or intensity-modulated proton therapy (n=20). Treated nodal and subclinical regions received 30 Gy in 15 fractions and a sequential boost of 40 Gy in 20 fractions. The 5-year results showed that 260 patients had no evidence of disease at 5 years and 250 were alive at last follow-up. Five-year outcomes were: Locoregional control: 97.0% OS: 90.8% Progression-free survival: 85.9% DMFS: 91.2% A single elective nodal failure occurred 6 months after concurrent CRT in a contralateral indeterminate lymph node present at baseline and treated with 30 Gy, the authors reported. The last regional failure occurred 18 months post-treatment. Distant-only recurrences occurred in 23 patients. At last follow-up, 12 of the patients remained alive with no evidence of disease, and one remained alive with disease. Please enable JavaScript to view the comments powered by Disqus. analysis.brief_en: A study published on November 3, 2026, by MedPage Today highlights long-term outcomes of de-escalated treatment for HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer. The research, conducted at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City, involved 276 patients who received a reduced radiation dose of 30 Gy for elective nodal irradiation (ENI) instead of the standard 50-60 Gy. After a median follow-up of 5 years, 94% of patients were alive without evidence of disease, and 90.8% had overall survival. The study showed that omitting low-risk nodal regions did not lead to treatment failures, with 97.0% locoregional control and 91.2% distant metastasis-free survival. However, the authors emphasize that this regimen still needs confirmation in a multicenter phase III trial to establish it as a standard of care. The findings suggest that reducing radiation doses can significantly improve patient outcomes while minimizing toxic effects, particularly in HPV-associated OPC, which is known to be sensitive to cisplatin-based chemotherapy. The study also notes that advanced imaging techniques like PET-CT and MRI may help identify smaller lymph nodes that require higher radiation doses, ensuring effective treatment without unnecessary exposure.

news.content_zh: MedPage Today 于 2026 年 11 月 3 日发表的一项研究强调了 治疗 降级治疗 HPV 阳性口咽癌的长期结果。这项研究是在纽约市纪念斯隆凯特琳癌症中心进行的,涉及 276 名患者,他们接受了 30 Gy 的选择性淋巴结照射 (ENI) 辐射剂量,而不是标准的 50-60 Gy。中位随访 5 年后,94% 的患者在没有疾病证据的情况下仍存活,90.8% 的患者总体存活。研究表明,省略低风险淋巴结区域不会导致 治疗 失败,局部区域控制率为 97.0%,无远处转移生存率为 91.2%。然而,作者强调,该方案仍需要在多中心 III 期试验中得到证实,以将其确立为护理标准。研究结果表明,减少辐射剂量可以显着改善患者的治疗效果,同时最大限度地减少毒性作用,特别是在 HPV 相关的 OPC 中,已知这种 OPC 对顺铂化疗敏感。研究还指出,PET-CT 和 MRI 等先进成像技术可能有助于识别需要更高辐射剂量的较小淋巴结,确保 治疗 有效,而不会造成不必要的暴露。

Infectious Disease > General Infectious Disease Novel Therapy Lands Speedy Approval for Wart-Like Airway Disease — Plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy reduced surgery need in recurrent respiratory papillomatosis by Terrence Rudd, Staff Writer, MedPage Today November 2, 2026 • 2 min read Add MedPage Today on Google MedpageToday The FDA granted accelerated approval to doruxapapogene ralaplasmid and lalikinogene sifuplasmid (Voceryq) opens in a new tab or windowto reduce the frequency of surgical papilloma excisions in adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP), the agency announced late on Friday. As the first FDA-approved recombinant plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy, doruxapapogene ralaplasmid-lalikinogene sifuplasmid targets the wart-like growths that characterize RRP. The growths are caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) and develop in the airways, particularly around the larynx. Severe cases of the rare disease can spread into the respiratory tract and make breathing difficult. There is no cure, but repeated surgeries can remove growths if they return. FDA based its decision on efficacy data from RRP-001, a phase I/II clinical trialopens in a new tab or window. The open-label trial included 32 patients who'd undergone at least two surgeries in the prior year to remove RRP growths. Among 26 patients who had at least three surgeries in the 12 months before treatment, 27% had a complete response to the plasmid therapy, defined as requiring no surgical excisions during 12 months of follow-up. "The approval of Voceryq is an important step in improving the quality of life for RRP patients as every surgery carries the risk of laryngeal injury," said investigator Simon Best, MD, of Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, in a statementopens in a new tab or window from manufacturer Inovio Pharmaceuticals. "I believe it is in the best interest of RRP patients that the standard of care quickly transition away from surgical interventions to immunotherapy after RRP is diagnosed." Doruxapapogene ralaplasmid-lalikinogene sifuplasmid includes two plasmids that contain genetic coding for HPV proteins and interleukin 12. Patients' own healthy cells transcribe that coding to stimulate immune system attacks against cells infected with the HPV types 6 and 11 that cause RRP. The therapy's treatment regimenopens in a new tab or window begins with surgical debulking of visible papilloma, followed by an intramuscular dose of the plasmid therapy every 3 weeks for a total of four doses. Label warnings include potential adverse events (AEs) such as muscle contractions, transient bleeding, and vasovagal reactions. The most common AEs in trials included injection site reactions, headache, fatigue, hypertension, nausea, and dizziness. The new treatment was approved in combination with a proprietary DNA medicine delivery device (CELLECTRA 5PSP). Postmarketing trials will be required to verify and describe the therapy's clinical benefit. The FDA approved the immunotherapy zopapogene imadenovec (Papzimeos)opens in a new tab or window for RRP in 2025, the first approved medical therapy for the condition. Infectious Disease > General Infectious Disease Novel Therapy Lands Speedy Approval for Wart-Like Airway Disease — Plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy reduced surgery need in recurrent respiratory papillomatosis by Terrence Rudd, Staff Writer, MedPage Today November 2, 2026 • 2 min read Add MedPage Today on Google MedpageToday The FDA granted accelerated approval to doruxapapogene ralaplasmid and lalikinogene sifuplasmid (Voceryq) opens in a new tab or windowto reduce the frequency of surgical papilloma excisions in adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP), the agency announced late on Friday. As the first FDA-approved recombinant plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy, doruxapapogene ralaplasmid-lalikinogene sifuplasmid targets the wart-like growths that characterize RRP. The growths are caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) and develop in the airways, particularly around the larynx. Severe cases of the rare disease can spread into the respiratory tract and make breathing difficult. There is no cure, but repeated surgeries can remove growths if they return. FDA based its decision on efficacy data from RRP-001, a phase I/II clinical trialopens in a new tab or window. The open-label trial included 32 patients who'd undergone at least two surgeries in the prior year to remove RRP growths. Among 26 patients who had at least three surgeries in the 12 months before treatment, 27% had a complete response to the plasmid therapy, defined as requiring no surgical excisions during 12 months of follow-up. "The approval of Voceryq is an important step in improving the quality of life for RRP patients as every surgery carries the risk of laryngeal injury," said investigator Simon Best, MD, of Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, in a statementopens in a new tab or window from manufacturer Inovio Pharmaceuticals. "I believe it is in the best interest of RRP patients that the standard of care quickly transition away from surgical interventions to immunotherapy after RRP is diagnosed." Doruxapapogene ralaplasmid-lalikinogene sifuplasmid includes two plasmids that contain genetic coding for HPV proteins and interleukin 12. Patients' own healthy cells transcribe that coding to stimulate immune system attacks against cells infected with the HPV types 6 and 11 that cause RRP. The therapy's treatment regimenopens in a new tab or window begins with surgical debulking of visible papilloma, followed by an intramuscular dose of the plasmid therapy every 3 weeks for a total of four doses. Label warnings include potential adverse events (AEs) such as muscle contractions, transient bleeding, and vasovagal reactions. The most common AEs in trials included injection site reactions, headache, fatigue, hypertension, nausea, and dizziness. The new treatment was approved in combination with a proprietary DNA medicine delivery device (CELLECTRA 5PSP). Postmarketing trials will be required to verify and describe the therapy's clinical benefit. The FDA approved the immunotherapy zopapogene imadenovec (Papzimeos)opens in a new tab or window for RRP in 2025, the first approved medical therapy for the condition. news.content_title: Govt eyes HPV vaccination for boys amid low second-dose uptake among girls
news.content: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 3 – The government is considering extending the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination programme to boys as Kenya steps up efforts to prevent cervical cancer and other HPV-related diseases. Medical Services Principal Secretary Ouma Oluga said vaccinating boys could become an important part of the country’s long-term disease prevention strategy, although the current programme remains focused on girls. His remarks come amid concerns over low completion rates for the HPV vaccine among girls, with the latest Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey showing that only 20 per cent have received the recommended second dose. The survey found that 59 per cent of girls had received at least one dose of the HPV vaccine, an increase from 30 per cent recorded in the 2022 survey. However, the significant drop between first-dose and second-dose coverage raises concerns about Kenya’s ability to ensure that more girls complete the recommended vaccination schedule. Oluga acknowledged that more efforts are needed to strengthen HPV vaccination and expand protection against the virus among young people. He said the government could consider extending the programme to boys in the future, describing it as an important area for further attention. “Maybe in the future, we will also consider vaccinating boys,” Oluga said. The PS also highlighted the burden of cervical cancer in Kenya, saying the disease affects approximately 7,000 women every year. Cervical cancer is largely caused by persistent infection with high-risk types of HPV, a common virus primarily transmitted through sexual contact. HPV vaccination before exposure to the virus offers the strongest protection against infection and related diseases. While HPV vaccination programmes have traditionally prioritised girls because of the vaccine’s role in preventing cervical cancer, vaccinating boys can also help reduce transmission and protect them against other HPV-related conditions, including certain cancers. The latest survey figures suggest that Kenya has made progress in increasing access to the first HPV vaccine dose, with coverage rising from 30 per cent in 2022 to 59 per cent. However, the fact that only 20 per cent of girls have received the second dose points to persistent challenges in follow-up, public awareness and access to vaccination services. Expanding the programme to boys would require additional planning and resources, with the government yet to announce a timeline for the proposed intervention. Oluga’s remarks therefore signal a possible future policy direction rather than an immediate change to the national HPV vaccination programme. DAVIS AYEGA

QQ空间 去年年底,我国将HPV疫苗纳入免疫规划,符合条件的女孩可全程免费接种二价HPV疫苗。大江资讯记者日前从市卫健委获悉,截至目前,全市适龄女孩免费HPV疫苗接种覆盖率达47.8%。 据介绍,宫颈癌是最常见的妇科恶性肿瘤,主要是由高危型人乳头瘤病毒持续感染引起,也是目前病因明确、可防可控的癌症。及时接种HPV疫苗是宫颈癌防控的第一道防线,我国约70%的宫颈癌与HPV-16和HPV-18两种高危型别病毒感染相关,二价HPV疫苗可有效预防这两种型别病毒感染,是未成年女孩健康防护的“刚需疫苗”。 同时,HPV疫苗的安全性已有大量研究和实际接种数据支持,目前我国上市的二价、四价和九价HPV疫苗均不含活病毒和激素,不会引起HPV感染,也不会因接种疫苗而致癌。 我市认真落实国家部署要求,所有免疫规划接种点全面开放周末接种服务,方便学生和家长安排时间。市卫健委、市教育局、市妇联联合发布《致芜湖市全体适龄女生家长的一封信》,传递科学、规范的疫苗接种理念。各县区疾控部门、接种单位同步下沉服务,通过开设咨询专线、门诊面对面答疑、社区义诊等方式,为适龄女生及家长提供专业接种指导。 此外,如果适龄女孩已自费接种四价、九价HPV疫苗,也视同完成了免疫规划疫苗接种,不需要重复接种。适龄女孩家长可以综合考虑孩子的健康需求等实际情况,选择接种免费的国家免疫规划疫苗,或自费接种四价、九价疫苗。 目前,我市二价、九价等各价型疫苗储备充足、调配有序,适龄女孩可根据疾控部门和学校的安排,前往附近的社区卫生服务中心、乡镇卫生院进行接种。 接种适用人群:出生日期在2011年11月10日以后且接种当日已满13周岁的适龄女孩。全程免费接种2针,2针间隔时间为6个月,因故延迟接种不影响最终免疫效果。 接种前须知:必须由家长或法定监护人陪同到场,不可由孩子独自前往;随身携带儿童预防接种证、有效身份证件(户口本、身份证均可);主动告知医生孩子既往过敏史、近期身体状况、既往接种不良反应。 接种后护理要点:接种完毕后,需在门诊现场留观30分钟,无头晕、皮疹、严重不适方可离开;出现接种部位轻微红肿硬结、手臂短暂酸痛、乏力,1—3日便可自行缓解,无需紧张。 海量资讯、精准解读,尽在新浪财经APP 新浪财经声明:此消息系转载自合作媒体,新浪财经登载此文出于传递更多信息之目的,文章内容仅供参考,不构成投资建议。 文章关键词: 新冠肺炎 0条评论|0人参与网友评论 表情 登录|注册 |退出 腾讯QQ QQ空间 去年年底,我国将HPV疫苗纳入免疫规划,符合条件的女孩可全程免费接种二价HPV疫苗。大江资讯记者日前从市卫健委获悉,截至目前,全市适龄女孩免费HPV疫苗接种覆盖率达47.8%。 据介绍,宫颈癌是最常见的妇科恶性肿瘤,主要是由高危型人乳头瘤病毒持续感染引起,也是目前病因明确、可防可控的癌症。及时接种HPV疫苗是宫颈癌防控的第一道防线,我国约70%的宫颈癌与HPV-16和HPV-18两种高危型别病毒感染相关,二价HPV疫苗可有效预防这两种型别病毒感染,是未成年女孩健康防护的“刚需疫苗”。 同时,HPV疫苗的安全性已有大量研究和实际接种数据支持,目前我国上市的二价、四价和九价HPV疫苗均不含活病毒和激素,不会引起HPV感染,也不会因接种疫苗而致癌。 我市认真落实国家部署要求,所有免疫规划接种点全面开放周末接种服务,方便学生和家长安排时间。市卫健委、市教育局、市妇联联合发布《致芜湖市全体适龄女生家长的一封信》,传递科学、规范的疫苗接种理念。各县区疾控部门、接种单位同步下沉服务,通过开设咨询专线、门诊面对面答疑、社区义诊等方式,为适龄女生及家长提供专业接种指导。 此外,如果适龄女孩已自费接种四价、九价HPV疫苗,也视同完成了免疫规划疫苗接种,不需要重复接种。适龄女孩家长可以综合考虑孩子的健康需求等实际情况,选择接种免费的国家免疫规划疫苗,或自费接种四价、九价疫苗。 目前,我市二价、九价等各价型疫苗储备充足、调配有序,适龄女孩可根据疾控部门和学校的安排,前往附近的社区卫生服务中心、乡镇卫生院进行接种。 接种适用人群:出生日期在2011年11月10日以后且接种当日已满13周岁的适龄女孩。全程免费接种2针,2针间隔时间为6个月,因故延迟接种不影响最终免疫效果。 接种前须知:必须由家长或法定监护人陪同到场,不可由孩子独自前往;随身携带儿童预防接种证、有效身份证件(户口本、身份证均可);主动告知医生孩子既往过敏史、近期身体状况、既往接种不良反应。 接种后护理要点:接种完毕后,需在门诊现场留观30分钟,无头晕、皮疹、严重不适方可离开;出现接种部位轻微红肿硬结、手臂短暂酸痛、乏力,1—3日便可自行缓解,无需紧张。 海量资讯、精准解读,尽在新浪财经APP 新浪财经声明:此消息系转载自合作媒体,新浪财经登载此文出于传递更多信息之目的,文章内容仅供参考,不构成投资建议。 文章关键词: 新冠肺炎 0条评论|0人参与网友评论 表情 登录|注册 |退出
